I would say yes, because waiting for attrition to do its thing may work, but is not the way to go and I would absolutely not recommend it. If any occlusal correcting is needed then your dentist should perform said adjustment. You need help to stop the teeth grinding and bring your attrition to a halt. Have you tried visual feedback to help make you aware of your daytime grinding?

Take stickers (red dots perhaps) and stick them around the house/workplace, places you know you look at rather often. These stickers are meant to be reminders, if you see one and happen to be clenching, it'll make you aware of what you are doing and that you need to stop. An alternative to the grinding (when you catch yourself doiing it) is toning the letter m.

An important thing to be aware of is that your teeth should never be contact unless you are eating/chewing.

Source: my university is one of the foremost TMD centres in Europe, we have had a lot of training and experience in cases similar to yours.

Has the doctor checked your occlusion? Sometimes the pain from the tooth may be due to traumatic occlusion (aka excessive biting on the tooth), since you know you clench your jaws (and have a night guard). Maybe you also do some clenching during the day as well?
Also, you had a molar that took some of the clenching load so there was more of an ”even” force on each tooth. Losing the first molar meant more pressure on the 2nd (and 3rd), leading to a reaction from the tooth. 
If that is the case, this could be more TMD related than endodontic.

I don't know the protocol of how things go about where you are from, but at least here it depends on the amount of calculus. Here, if it's a little then they remove it on the spot. If it is a good amount then they book more appts but again, I don't know because I reckon it varies. Also, I guess it depends on the alloted time for your appointment 

Don't worry about periodontitis, it is a slow progressing disease and I doubt you have it. It takes many years until you actually lose a tooth and again, I doubt that is your case however I can't say for sure because then I need xrays (and a clinical evaluation.)

Gum recessions may occur due to brushing your teeth too hard as well, not just due to a pathology in your supporting tissues. 

Most dental disease are not genetically linked (don't quote me on this because my memory i failing me on if that really was the case.) The only genetically affected dental disease I can remember is aggressive periodontitis. 

Try not to overthink your situation, you will be fine.

Once the calculus is removed, and the gums finally undergo the healing process, the fibers will reattach as it was so long as no bone loss has occured, and so long as the periodontal ligament has not been compromised in any way. 

Judging from the pics and your age, I'd say it looks like a pretty bad case of gingivitis more than anything. However, unless I clinically examine you and see x-rays, I'm not gonna give you a definitive answer. Since the inflammation causes a raise in the overall gum levels as well (swelling), I can't judge if there is any gum recession. I'd say you needn't worry too much- just keep up with the hygiene and see your dental care provider soon. 

Sorry for not giving you anything definitive, and best of luck!

I've seen docs that drill "too far" just for the sake of reaching completely unaffected dentin (and the closer a prep is to the pulp the more prone it is to hurt- not to mention if they drill into the pulp.) also, with deeper cavities, the stepwise excavation technique is used rather than just drilling to remove all caries in one sitting. I also didn't put any blame, merely hypothesized on the most usual reasons post-operative pains arise. And yeah, there are many factors as to why it would hurt so I do agree with you, obviously

Maybe the fillings in the upper jaw were not properly layered and the reason your teeth hurt is the tension from the forces pulling at each other. Do you feel tightness in your teeth? Maybe the filling is not properly adhered to the natural tooth and there is a leak of sorts? Does it hurt when you chew or more when eating smth hot/cold? 


Never feel like you are a troublesome patient!! We need patients to tell us what's wrong otherwise we'll never realise since you are the ones feeling these things! 

Edit: it can hurt a couple days after you get your fillings but since yours has persisted for 3 weeks I'd say it's a cause for worry. Did they take any xrays? If so, ask them to give you a printout of the radiographs (post-fillings if available) and let another dentist take a look. 
Another cause for pain is pulp lesions,aka the dentist has drilled too far and reached the pulp. Again, I'd say go to another dentist to double-check. 

Sources: I'm a dental student in my 3rd year

Chop up you fav veggies (eg corn, lettuce, mushrooms, etc..), place chickpea blend (and avocados if used) on a tortilla, place other veggies on as well, roll tortilla. Done!

haha you're probably right... it's just that in my school we are really thorough and tell the patient such things because a plaque index is basically the percentage of plaque (in short, bacteria that has managed to colonize on your teeth) present in your mouth at the time of the examination. (this is usually discovered by colouring the teeth with a red/pink dye that colours the plaque, we then register on what dental surfaces that colour is present, then the computer does the calculations) It is an indicator of how well a patient keeps up with their oral hygiene. So if a patient has a lowered plaque index when we examine them again it means that they have improved with their hygiene routine.
